nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the realist novel of poverty and the literary profession
literary_identity: Novelist; the great English novelist of the struggling writer and of the urban poor of the 1880s-90s.
biography: Born at Wakefield on 22 November 1857, the son of a chemist; he was a brilliant scholar at Owens College, Manchester, but was expelled and imprisoned for a month in 1876 after stealing money to help a young woman, Nell Harrison, whom he later married. He lived in London and then in the United States (1876-77), returned and married twice more, and supported himself by tutoring and by writing. He wrote twenty-three novels, of which New Grub Street (1891) and The Odd Women (1893) are the best known, and he died at Saint-Jean-de-Luz in France on 28 December 1903.
literary_profile: Gissing wrote the English novel of the failed intellectual: his subject is the educated man or woman without money, condemned to grind in the literary marketplace or in the genteel poverty of the lodging-house. He is a realist of a peculiarly bleak kind, precise about rents, wages, publishers' advances and the cost of respectability, and his best work is a permanent record of the London of the 1880s. He is also, in The Odd Women, one of the first English novelists to take the surplus of unmarried women seriously as a social problem rather than a joke.
stylistic_characteristics: Grim documentary realism; exact accounting of money, food and rent; the interior monologue of disappointed intelligence; irony verging on despair; London fog, lodging-houses, reading-rooms and offices; a classical, fastidious prose set against sordid material.
intellectual_concerns: Poverty and the shame of the educated poor; the literary marketplace and the prostitution of talent; marriage as an economic transaction; the 'odd women' and female self-support; class, education and the failure of aspiration; the city as a machine of isolation.
historical_significance: Gissing is the finest English novelist of the literary profession and of lower-middle-class poverty in the 1880s: New Grub Street is the founding novel about the writer's market, and The Odd Women is a central text in the history of English feminism. His work influenced Orwell, who wrote an essay on him, and the twentieth-century novel of the unsuccessful writer.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the slum novel and the detective story
literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the chronicler of the East End and the creator of the first English professional private detective.
biography: Born in the East End of London on 1 November 1863, the son of an engine fitter; he left school at sixteen and worked as a clerk at the People's Palace in Mile End, where he began writing and where his first sketches of East End life were composed. Tales of Mean Streets (1894) and A Child of the Jago (1896) made him the leading English writer of slum fiction; he later became a connoisseur and collector of Japanese art and wrote little fiction after 1911. He died at Chalfont St Peter, Buckinghamshire, on 4 December 1945.
literary_profile: Morrison wrote the East End from inside: his Jago is not an exotic hell but a precise topographical and economic reality, and his refusal to sentimentalise it made him controversial with both the philanthropists and the socialists. He is also, in Martin Hewitt, the inventor of the English professional private detective who works with the police rather than against them — a deliberate, bureaucratic answer to Sherlock Holmes.
stylistic_characteristics: Cockney dialect rendered phonetically and with great care; topographical exactness (street names, courts, public houses); short, hard sentences; refusal of moral commentary; documentary detail of rents, trades and food.
intellectual_concerns: Poverty, criminality and environment; the 'street' as a social organism; philanthropy and its failures; the professional detective and the police; class and the East End; race and the Chinese and Jewish communities of the docks.
historical_significance: Morrison is the central English novelist of the East End slum in the 1890s and a key figure in the transition from the Victorian social-problem novel to the twentieth-century working-class novel. A Child of the Jago was the most discussed English novel of 1896, and Martin Hewitt is a foundational figure in the history of the English detective story.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; political economy, social analysis and the novel of ideas
literary_identity: Sociologist, political economist, journalist and novelist; the first woman to earn a living by the Victorian periodical press and the great populariser of political economy.
biography: Born at Norwich on 12 June 1802 into a Unitarian family of manufacturers; she lost most of the family fortune in 1829 and began writing to support herself, publishing Illustrations of Political Economy (1832-34), which sold in enormous numbers. She travelled to America in 1834-36 and wrote Society in America (1837) and Retrospect of Western Travel (1838) after a tour of the slave states that made her an abolitionist. She wrote thirty-five books, translated Comte, edited a periodical, and after 1855 lived at Ambleside, where she wrote leaders for the Daily News while ill. She died at Ambleside on 27 June 1876.
literary_profile: Martineau invented the popular social-science essay and the sociological travel book. Her Illustrations of Political Economy are fictional case studies designed to teach the new science of political economy to ordinary readers; Society in America and its companion volume are among the founding texts of English sociology, and her Autobiography is one of the most exact self-portraits in the language. She wrote as an authority, not as a lady, and she made the position of women, the poor and the slave the test cases of social analysis.
stylistic_characteristics: The exemplary narrative with a documented argument; the plain declarative sentence; the systematic division into topics; the use of statistics and first-hand observation; the leader and the review essay as forms of public education.
intellectual_concerns: Political economy and the condition of the working classes; slavery and abolition; the position of women and the marriage law; education; the comparative study of religions and of society; the authority of the woman writer.
historical_significance: Martineau is the founding English woman sociologist and one of the inventors of the modern profession of journalism: she made political economy a subject for the general reader, wrote the most important English book on American society before Tocqueville's readership was established, and helped to shape the feminist argument of the 1830s-50s. Her Autobiography is a classic of Victorian self-writing.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-English; the periodical essay, polemic and social criticism
literary_identity: Essayist, feminist and animal-rights campaigner; one of the most important Victorian writers on the position of women and the founder of the English anti-vivisection movement.
biography: Born near Dublin on 4 December 1822, the daughter of a landed Irish family; she was educated at home, left the family home after a quarrel over her refusal of orthodox religion, and worked as a governess before inheriting an income in 1857. She wrote for the Westminster Review, the Fortnightly and the Contemporary, campaigned for the Married Women's Property Acts and against the Contagious Diseases Acts, and in 1875 founded the Society for the Protection of Animals Liable to Vivisection. She lived for thirty-six years with the sculptor Mary Lloyd and died at Hengwrt, Wales, on 5 April 1904.
literary_profile: Cobbe wrote the Victorian essay as an instrument of political argument: she was the most important woman publicist between Martineau and Mill's circle, and her essays on 'Wife-Torture in England' (1878), 'The Final Cause of Woman' and 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors' turned the periodical press into a feminist platform. Her later work on animal ethics made her the founder of English philosophical argument for animal rights.
stylistic_characteristics: The documented essay with statistics and case evidence; the reasoned petition; vivid narrative case histories; a direct, forceful plain style; the moral appeal over the head of the specialism.
intellectual_concerns: The legal position of women and the married woman's property; wife-beating and the courts; the Contagious Diseases Acts and the double standard; education and women's paid work; animal suffering and the ethics of experimental science; religion and conscience.
historical_significance: Cobbe is a founding figure of English feminism and of the animal-rights movement: 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors' is one of the most effective pieces of Victorian feminist polemic, her evidence to the Royal Commission on wife-beating helped to change the law, and her anti-vivisection writing is the origin of the modern philosophical case against animal experimentation.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the pamphlet, the speech and the literature of social reform
literary_identity: Reformer and writer; the leader of the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts and one of the great Victorian prose writers of moral outrage.
biography: Born at Milfield, Northumberland, on 13 April 1828, the daughter of a cousin of the Earl of Shaftesbury; she married the clergyman George Butler in 1852 and after the death of their daughter in 1864 turned to public work. From 1869 she led the Ladies' National Association for the Repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts, campaigned against the state regulation of prostitution, and after the Acts were suspended in 1883 and repealed in 1886 she campaigned against the traffic in women in Europe. She died at Wooler, Northumberland, on 30 December 1906.
literary_profile: Butler wrote the literature of moral agitation: speeches, pamphlets, letters and a remarkable body of periodical prose in which the language of Evangelical religion is turned into a weapon against the state. Her subject is the double standard made law — the Acts subjected women to examination and registration while leaving their clients untouched — and her argument is that a law which treats a woman as a thing cannot be accepted by any Christian or any citizen.
stylistic_characteristics: Prophetic, impassioned oratory in print; the personal address and the appeal to conscience; the concrete case and the direct quotation; the use of religious language against legal authority; the pamphlet as a political instrument.
intellectual_concerns: The state regulation of prostitution and the double standard; the traffic in women; the rights of the subject under the law; Christian conscience against state policy; the position of women in public life; the Empire and the colonial extension of the Acts.
historical_significance: Butler is one of the most important British social reformers of the nineteenth century and a major writer of Victorian polemic: her campaign repealed the Contagious Diseases Acts (1886) and her international work shaped the first international conventions against the traffic in women. Her biography of Catherine of Siena and her pamphlets are read as classics of Victorian religious feminism.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the pamphlet, the secularist lecture and the socialist essay
literary_identity: Freethinker, socialist, trade-union organiser and later theosophist; one of the most effective radical orators and polemicists of the 1880s.
biography: Born Annie Wood in London on 1 October 1847, the daughter of an Irish doctor; she married the clergyman Frank Besant in 1867 and separated from him in 1873 after refusing to continue in orthodox belief. She became a secularist lecturer, edited the National Reformer with Charles Bradlaugh, was prosecuted with him in 1877 for publishing a birth-control pamphlet, led the matchgirls' strike at Bryant and May in 1888 and was elected to the London School Board in 1888. She joined the Theosophical Society in 1889 and later settled in India, where she founded the Central Hindu College and became the first woman president of the Indian National Congress in 1917. She died at Adyar, Madras, on 20 September 1933.
literary_profile: Besant's early writing is the literature of freethought and of the new socialism: the pamphlet, the public lecture and the radical essay, written in a plain, forceful, argumentative prose designed to be read aloud and to convert. Her 1880s work on behalf of the matchgirls and the unemployed of the East End made her the most prominent woman radical in Britain, and her autobiography is a classic record of Victorian unbelief and self-making.
stylistic_characteristics: Direct argument and plain diction; the platform address with its rhythm and repetition; the polemical pamphlet; the reasoned appeal to evidence against scripture; the first-person narrative of conversion and release.
intellectual_concerns: Freethought and biblical criticism; birth control and the position of women; poverty, sweated labour and the rights of the unskilled worker; socialism and the land; education; the spiritual and the occult.
historical_significance: Besant is one of the most important British radical writers of the 1870s-80s: her trial with Bradlaugh established the right to publish birth-control literature, she founded the matchgirls' union, and she was a central figure in the early British socialist movement before her later career in India and the Theosophical Society.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; aesthetic criticism and the prose of art
literary_identity: Essayist and critic; the founder of English aesthetic criticism and the master of the Victorian prose of sensation.
biography: Born at Stepney on 4 August 1839, the son of a surgeon; he was educated at King's School, Canterbury, and at Queen's College, Oxford, where he took a second class in 1862 and remained as a fellow of Brasenose from 1864. He published Studies in the History of the Renaissance in 1873, the book that gave the aesthetic movement its creed; Marius the Epicurean (1885) was his only completed novel, and he published Imaginary Portraits (1887), Appreciations (1889), Plato and Platonism (1893) and the posthumous Greek Studies (1895). He lived quietly at Oxford, a legend among undergraduates, and died there on 30 July 1894.
literary_profile: Pater's prose is the most musical and the most deliberate in Victorian criticism: he wrote to convey the sensation of a work of art rather than a judgment on it, and his famous 'Conclusion' to The Renaissance — that we are to burn always with a hard, gem-like flame and that art gives the highest quality to our moments as they pass — became the manifesto of the 1890s. His criticism is historical and psychological at once, and his fiction invents the imaginary portrait, the exemplary life rendered as a study in feeling.
stylistic_characteristics: Rhythmical, suspended sentences; the cadenced clause and the carefully withheld verb; sensuous and exact description of art; the essay as a meditation; the imaginary portrait and the imagined life; a refusal of moral summary.
intellectual_concerns: The transience of experience and the value of the moment; art and sensation; Hellenism and the pagan sensibility against Christian asceticism; the Renaissance as a rebirth of the senses; the education of the soul; style as a form of knowledge.
historical_significance: Pater is the founder of English aesthetic criticism and the prose writer who shaped Wilde, Yeats, Proust's reading of English prose and the whole literature of the 1890s. The Renaissance is one of the most influential books of Victorian England, and Marius the Epicurean is the finest English novel of ideas of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; criticism, the Renaissance history and the literature of desire
literary_identity: Critic, historian of the Renaissance and poet; the author of Renaissance in Italy and one of the founders of the modern literature of male same-sex desire.
biography: Born at Bristol on 5 October 1840, the son of a physician; he was educated at Harrow and Balliol College, Oxford, where he fell in love with a Bristol chorister and wrote the sonnets that became part of his life's secret work. He married Janet North in 1864 and lived at Clifton and Davos, Switzerland, for his health. He wrote Renaissance in Italy (1875-86), biographies of Michelangelo and Ben Jonson, translations of Greek poetry and a large body of verse and prose on Greek love. He died at Rome on 19 April 1893.
literary_profile: Symonds wrote the history of the Renaissance as a history of feeling: his seven-volume Renaissance in Italy is the first full English account of the period as a whole, and his studies of Greek ethics, Walt Whitman and Michelangelo were the foundation of the modern study of same-sex desire in literature. He was a poet of considerable power and a prose writer of great range, and his private writings — the Memoirs and the 'A Problem in Greek Ethics' — are among the first sustained English arguments for the dignity of homosexual love.
stylistic_characteristics: Historical narrative on a large scale; biography as psychological analysis; the sonnet and the elegy; scholarly prose with a personal urgency; the translation as an act of identification; private manuscript and careful publication.
intellectual_concerns: The Renaissance and its culture of the individual; Greek ethics and the love of men; the relation of art to sexuality; Whitman and democratic comradeship; Italy and the Alps as scenes of self-discovery; the ethics of concealment.
historical_significance: Symonds wrote the first comprehensive English history of the Italian Renaissance and was the most important English writer on same-sex desire before Wilde's trials: his 'A Problem in Greek Ethics' (privately printed, 1883) is a founding text of the modern discourse, and his influence on Pater, Gosse, Havelock Ellis and the 1890s is decisive.
